en: Preface to the Thousand Pines Notes:
Contemplating the Discourses of Śākyamuni Buddha on Benefiting Sentient Beings Over Forty-nine Years.
He has thoroughly cleansed his very heart and entrails so that they may respond to myriad exigencies; how could there be such filthiness as to clog the bowels of others? Let it be so.

A person attains Buddhahood. During the forty-nine years [following his enlightenment], he used solely this single, perfectly integrated, unimpeded, inconceivable, and pure mind as his eloquence to show people the place where they may establish their bodies and lives.

It is like a dragon-spirit appearing amidst the clouds, moving with divine transformations, and bringing forth rain as the clouds drift. Those who observe skillfully see the true body of the dragon; those who do not observe skillfully merely perceive—
Paper, ink, and written characters—therefore, the Tathāgata’s writing is not writing, and the Tathāgata’s speech is not speech.

Through transformative spiritualization, every word is the true essence, and every utterance radiates brilliance. Thus it is said that during the forty-nine years [of his teaching], he never spoke a single word.
Upon seeing that the World-Honored One’s very heart and entrails were pure, one is made to realize it directly and immediately, without being deceived by others. This is complete.
How could one such as Yan [Shouduan] be willing to consume the dregs of others or examine their spittle?
When Yunmen saw Śākyamuni pointing at heaven and pointing at earth, he immediately said, "If I had seen him then, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to the dogs.
He took that which belonged to the World-Honored One, overturned it, and manifested his own original face; how could he be willing to eat the leftovers of others' soup or rice? Such is the case.
To realize that existence is impermanent is barely sufficient to transcend the world; yet this must be achieved by one who is truly capable.

If you have not yet penetrated the profound mystery of the ultimate path, your talk of "seeing the truth" is merely idle chatter. Intending to deceive others, you are in fact deceiving yourself. To inquire into such a person’s inner thoughts is to do nothing more than gloss over their lips.

They cannot clearly understand the capacity for transcendence inherent in the Buddha’s teaching. Words do not exceed the mind, and the mind does not exceed words; how could mind and words be two separate dharmas?
Yet, when one lets go completely at the precipice, they are unwilling to accept this realization. To know directly where one returns is to naturally achieve liberation.

Students vainly follow the literal text and pursue its meanings; the whole world clamors and pursues these distractions without awakening, like drinking from a fountain of madness, unaware of the truth.

The Buddhas and Patriarchs have bequeathed their words to directly reveal the fundamental essence and exhaustively resolve even the slightest doubts. Moving with ease in all directions according to their will, one may discern the school of Mind-Buddhism;
entering the ford of benefit without being defiled, these teachings flow solely from within one’s own breast to respond to the world.

As soon as the blade of wisdom is brandished, even the slightest doubt is instantly severed. It can serve as the way of the mundane world, and it can also be grasped as the way that transcends the world.
Mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas are fused into a single mass and blended into one whole.
It is possible to establish mundane phenomena; it is also possible to establish supramundane phenomena.
Apart from mundane phenomena, no supramundane phenomena can be found; apart from supramundane phenomena, no mundane phenomena can be found.
Nevertheless, even so, one may discern supramundane phenomena within mundane phenomena, and discern mundane phenomena within supramundane phenomena.
When worldly dharmas are neither confused nor rigid, one may truly be said to possess the eye.
Having overturned the nests of the sages and worthies and uprooted the ancestral styles of the Buddhas and patriarchs, one can enter the realm of demons and can enter the realm of Buddhas.
Unbound by worldly dharmas or world-transcending dharmas, one becomes free and easy; only then does one become a person of liberation. Once the jade has been carved...
Yet it remains within the uncut gem; the sword has been tempered and contains its radiance. Therefore, within every thought-moment, one sees all sentient beings attaining Buddhahood.
Whether there is a Buddha or not, that too is not the Buddha. Whether the mind has antiquity or modernity, that too is not the mind.
For this reason, the Elder Śākyamuni’s lifelong livelihood consists of untiring discourse, which he demonstrates to sentient beings; yet it cannot be found within the words of the teaching.
Above. Furthermore, it may be said that adding annotations is permissible for the sake of the mind and the Buddha.
Thousand Pines’ Notes:
Contemplating the Tathāgata’s magnificent writings of a thousand ages is like beholding the Tathāgata’s mind of a thousand ages. Thus, five...

The Celestial Language fills Jambudvīpa; its "Bird-Track" phonology is so perfect that it is difficult to penetrate through artificial analysis. To directly savor the resonance of the Brahma-sound, what need is there for the language of Tang?
Amidst paper, ink, and written characters, the empty, perfect, and wondrous response does not assume form of its own accord, yet its form is already revealed.
Originally there was no trace, yet the trace has already become manifest. The words transcend the realm of hearing and seeing; the principle lies beyond the reach of thought and deliberation.

The text expresses the mind, and the mind is revealed through the text. Worldly people seek the mind only through the text, yet who knows that the very manifestation of the mind is entirely composed of text?
Thus, the life-blood of the Tathāgata has been analyzed with exhaustive detail and laid bare without remainder, just as [the maps of] Yu were.
In his management of the waters and his employment of troops, Huaiyin’s strategies emerged with sudden brilliance; every shift was extraordinary.
Whether deploying or withdrawing, whether killing or giving life, none dared to face the sharpness of his edge. Not even the tip of a single sword could be provoked or touched.

He severed each and every one of the seventeen hundred tangles of rotten vines of conceptual views, so that both seeing and hearing were extinguished, and he went directly back to the time before a thousand kalpas. Together with...

All people see one another. Thus, when Yu governed the waters—whether it be the confluence of the nine rivers, surging currents, or suspended waterfalls that cannot be diverted or intercepted—all are like the Tathāgata’s single wisdom flowing forth as the twelvefold teaching, by means of which the twelvefold teaching [is established].
They all converge upon the one mind. This wondrous discourse for those of perfect capacity enters skillfully into the profound depths.
Tens of millions of words unfold like spreading clouds, all of them permeating the excellence of both emptiness and existence. They stand alone beyond the realm of written characters;
they are liberated far outside of words. All are "live phrases," utterly devoid of the scent of mere letters—being the very words yet not being words, being speech yet...
These are words, yet not mere verbal expressions; they are intended solely to lead people to realize that which existed ten thousand kalpas ago.
Be careful not to lose sight of the fundamental and abandon the source. Therefore, whether explained horizontally or vertically, one does not depart from this foundation.

At the moment of the simultaneous "pecking" and "puncturing," one silently realizes the purport of the sutras. Within this single flow of speech, what constitutes the school? What constitutes the teaching? What constitutes the mind?
Who is the Buddha? What is sudden, what is gradual? With effortless ease, he strikes the jar and sings;
his music flows so abundantly it fills the ears, its brilliance so radiant it overflows the eyes. Amidst this, all rejoice and find singular delight. At such a time as this—
Not knowing who are the Buddhas and who are sentient beings, one does not abide in goodness; what else, then, could one seek?

Therefore, the valley responds to the woodcutter’s song and the flowers welcome the birds’ laughter. To expand upon this and apply it further would be like adding legs to a snake—needlessly redundant.
Thus, Jue of Langya said: "The Way of our late master Fenyang was such that beneath Fenyang’s gate there was a 'Lion of Xihe.'"
He sits crouching at the gate; anyone who comes near is immediately bitten to death. By what skillful means can one enter the gate of Fenyang and see the person of Fenyang?
Here in Langya, there is likewise a lion that crouches on the ground;
if anyone comes, they lose their very body and life. By what skillful means can one enter the gate of Langya and see the person of Langya? These two—
A turning word. Only when people can examine it and extract its meaning does one possess the eye for discerning the Dharma.

If it were not so, there would be no place to settle oneself or establish one’s life. Therefore, I have let it flow from the tip of my brush; those who respond to the wind and follow the resonance will find their doubts and stagnations suddenly cleared away.

Were it not for a person of ultimate realization, how could one cut off the tongue at its root and bring this great matter of a thousand lives and a hundred kalpas to a conclusion? It is like traveling a thousand li—
A horse, driven by Sunyang, gallops past cities and over clods of earth, its swift current like a streak of shooting star.
In the *Chan Zong He Lun*,

it is said that from the time of the World-Honored One’s enlightenment under the morning star until before he held up the flower, for forty-nine years, his compassionate heart was too urgent as he directed himself toward people.
He spoke tens of millions of words with clamorous discourse; yet people can only read his dead words, unable to read his living words.

The Tathāgata breathes the void, the place where he awakens humanity. He points directly to the moment of opening the mouth, where there is no deliberation, no leakage, no carving or drilling, and no application of the mind.
It is like a dragon dwelling in the ocean, like a tiger in its lair.
In the forest, the wind and clouds thundered, and a hundred monsters were struck with awe.

The World-Honored One took that single moment of illumination he had attained while facing the morning star and brought it forth before everyone’s eyes, commanding all people to examine it thoroughly:
"Is this the twelvefold teaching spoken by the Tathāgata? Or is it the manifestation of his own mind? Since—
This is the teaching spoken by the Tathāgata. Why, then, do you say that for forty-nine years he never spoke a single word?

This is the very countenance of the Tathāgata’s own realization since time immemorial, cast forth in its entirety—the natural radiance of the original ground, the spontaneous perfection of celestial mechanism, the wondrous marks of the Tathāgata, free from any trace of whispered articulation, without discarding even the slightest fraction.
With power, he reveals his voice in harmony, manifesting his entire being to all sentient beings. His perfect capacity is suddenly revealed in his words;
gathering and releasing, his wondrous function flows freely in every direction. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are blended into a single, uniform essence.

Truth and falsehood, things and self—by raising one, all are fully encompassed, without distinction between sage and ordinary person. Neither lacking nor superfluous, he fuses the myriad dharmas into the one mind and realizes the thousand minds as one.

Within a single word, the songs of woodcutters and the chants of herdsmen—sounds and forms intermingling—are all clearly and simultaneously sealed. Expedient means and ultimate truth proceed together;

though the five schools diverge in their tenets and the three vehicles differ in their doctrinal characteristics, where can their meaning truly be lodged? When one probes the sharp edge of its function, it manifests in ten thousand transformations and a thousand wonders.
Exhausting principle and exhausting function, it is a seamless whole without beginning or end. There is not the slightest bit of leakage, nor is there a single dharma to be attained.
It is naturally vibrant and lively, ever-turning and flowing; it does not depart from the tip of the Tathāgata’s tongue.
It simply requires that all people penetrate this very covering, so that each may personally possess a segment of transcendent joy for as long as the sun and moon endure.
In a single month he drove forth wind and thunder; his tongue played with ease. Sometimes he composed in the style of the Classics, at other times he revealed fresh and elegant prose.

Whether establishing a school or expounding a doctrine, he was like one who cuts through crocodiles and dragons on the water or slays rhinoceroses and tigers on land. He strictly prohibited those who favored novelty or sought eccentricity, and deeply guarded against those who engaged in arbitrary interpretation.
Compared to the spiritual wonders of his thousands of scrolls, they were like a single autumn hair in the vast blue sea. Thus, without shedding a single drop of ink, he completed [his work].
All must surely cast out their brilliance; sheathing their tips and burying their points, they exhaust every possible human condition.
Indeed, when a person receives offerings from the various heavens, even a single flavor is tasted as being fully replete in every taste. Copper and iron are transformed into gold;

the marvelous is extracted from the putrid and corrupt. To observe words through the Way, and to observe the Way through words—thus one may perceive the Way, thus one may exhaustively master the Classics, and thus one may [attain realization].
Exerting one’s will, one can examine heaven and earth, understand ghosts and spirits, and penetrate the teachings of the hundred schools.
One opens the single eye of the crown of the head and releases the unsurpassed precious light. Who gains and who loses? Where should one go and from where should one depart?
Thus the First Patriarch said: "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and still. Such merit and virtue are not sought from the world; they must be truly realized."

Realizing the truth through practice is the actual application; it must not be mired in worldly mud. Regarding the sublime principle that transcends all, do not treat it as a mere public proclamation or a tangle of conceptual knots.
Now tell me: how can one speak without falling into the trap of life or death? How would you say it?
The Three Vehicles and the twelvefold division of the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are like the waters of the ocean, which have but one taste.
Reaching the highest and plunging the deepest, they surge as billows, swirl as ripples, roar as thunder, and spray as rain;

they can follow the dragon to transform the three thousand worlds—all these are the waves upon the tongue of the Tathāgata, vast and expansive in their discourse on the arts, emerging from the handiwork of the divine artisan.

In responding to capacities and providing instruction, whenever he encounters the opportune moment, he pours forth his realization with overflowing clarity. Unimpeded wherever he turns, he appears to divide and then re-unite, yet this does not diminish the majesty of the vast ocean.
Within his breast, there is no trace of conceptual shadows or attachments; rather, it is manifested right before his very eyes.
There is also no superior terminology; it is luminously and uniquely liberated. Only this void is vibrant and lively, possessing a sharp and resilient wind-bone, melting like springtime.
It is as if holding a scale within a mirror, or wind and thunder within one's grasp, yet responding appropriately to the affairs of the world.
There is no place where its spirit does not reach; therefore, Prajñā manifests before one. It is primordially complete and requires no cultivation or effort.
True wisdom is boundless, and the true mind is non-abiding; there is not the slightest leakage. Within the sphere of every person, it is fully present in each and every one.
Luoshan said: "The Mysterious Gate has no dharma; it establishes no regulations. It is like a king’s precious sword:
its sharp edge cannot be touched. To look at it is to blind one's eyes. There is not a single word that does not directly point upward;
there is not a single utterance that does not fully manifest the whole body. Thus, the Old Śākyamuni attained equal and right enlightenment in every place."
If there is a man of spirit who fixes his eye upon this point, he will immediately see that for himself, [the mind] moves freely in all directions without shifting so much as a hair’s breadth;
he will tread upon his own original source of life, which was never obtained from another.
One must, with intense alertness, gaze intently.
Now, those who observe the teachings but cannot observe the mind, yet those who can observe the mind are also able to harmonize with the teachings.
The teachings flow from the mind; the Tathāgata revealed the mind and thereby expounded the teachings. Sentient beings are deluded by the teachings and do not recognize the mind.
The teachings are the means of manifestation, while the mind is the master that expounds the teachings. To recognize [the mind]...
For one whose mind accords with the teaching, what further need is there to add even a single word to that mind? Indeed, not a single word can truly capture the reality of the situation.
Whether in a thousand words or a few phrases, when the mind is discussed face-to-face, it is clear and beyond doubt; it is serene and free from fear.

Yet, if one still cannot have confidence in this, and instead persists in holding to their own particular views, such efforts will ultimately fail to satisfy the original aspiration. To compare it to...

A door-knocking brick. Now that the gate has been opened, what further use is there for it? Why not observe the five-colored lightning radiating from the tip of the Tathāgata’s tongue—is this not the true mark of the Tathāgata?
His eloquence is inexhaustible; let those who seek the hidden mysteries have their way.
Pervading fragrance and sound yet dwelling nowhere, encompassing all of empty space as its measure, one may be deluded in seeking its source and remain ignorant of its end.
If one can truly know the mind, then the myriad dharmas all emerge from it. Pure, void, simple, and supreme—like hearing the music of Zheng and Wei, the meaning lies beyond words.
Though there are a thousand paths, they follow a single track; every thought-moment is not distinct. The heavens and earth are vast and expansive; their vertical establishment is not...
When a single thought-moment manifests before him, it issues forth spontaneously from the mouth; casting off the physical form entirely, the whole essence is revealed.
The natural radiance of the original ground is encountered face-to-face. Therefore, those who have stammered and hesitated for ten thousand generations find their foundation therein.
As for the unfolding of the scriptures, their purport transcends the words on the page. Those who read the Tathāgata’s words must simply attain clear and sudden enlightenment. Thus, Li Chang...
It is said: "The realms of infinite lands are not separated from oneself or others by so much as a hair’s tip;
the ten ages of past and present do not depart from this very moment of thought. When the spirit merges and the bones are saturated, the doubts of former kalpas dissolve like melting ice.
As for its literary brilliance, it reveals the very essence; as for its prosody, it resonates with perfect harmony. Thus, through repeated study—learning and unlearning alike—[the truth is realized].
My learning has also been leisurely. I have exhausted the teachings of the Tathāgata, yet not a single word remains in my breast;
I have neither read many words nor read few words. Therefore it is said: "The languages used for governing the world all accord with the True Dharma.

It is simply to pull out sentient beings from their various attachments, to push and break through their delusions and fixations, so that they neither cling to existence nor fall into non-existence, and thus penetrate beyond the barriers of names and forms.
Lí: To reveal one’s true heart upon the lips. If one relies on intellectual reasoning and views, there will ultimately remain a trace of something lacking in clarity.

Within the teachings, there are Sanskrit terms and their Chinese translations; whether they are explicit or esoteric explanations, all are the skillful means established by the Tathāgata for transformation.
The Dharma of the World-Honored One guides the course of fortune; through the Brahma-scriptures he establishes the school and reveals the mind as the teaching.
His words are the radiance of the torch of wisdom. Those who empty their bosoms draw from his lingering influence; those who rinse their mouths in his stream savor its remaining essence.
It is a sharp sword for dispelling consciousness and a precious blade for severing delusion. It resonates with the sound of the Dharma-conch, yet remains free from forced interpretation.

The term "Treasure" (Bǎo) has distinctions between the vernacular and the Sanskrit, yet the mind makes no distinction between the Tang and the Fan [languages]. Thus, the mind and its expression are like the whetstone and the blade;
the expression is to the mind as the blade is to the whetstone. The name "whetstone" is not the blade, and the name "blade" is not the whetstone.
One cannot discard the whetstone and still have a blade, nor can one discard the blade and still have a whetstone. It has never been heard that there is a blade...

When the handle is gone, the utility remains; when the utility is gone, the blade persists. Thus, one may say there is no distinction between the Tang and Indian [languages], yet the mind possesses the categories of conceptual thought.
How could it be that the Tang language can express meaning while the Sanskrit language cannot?

When conditions are exhausted and illumination is perfected, both the Exoteric and Esoteric are the One Mind—the provisional means by which the Tathāgata preached the Dharma to harmonize the wondrous nature of the mind, like a solitary crane.
"Empty and vast; the divine dragon plays in the sea.
Lan'an said, "Scholars of recent times do not awaken to this principle.

They assume that the Chan school is a distinct dharma-gate, such that those who take Chan as their primary focus are not following the Teaching, and those who take the Teaching as their primary focus are not practicing Chan. Consequently, they have created a duality."
Regarding these various theories of the household, they revile one another, clamoring and unable to restrain themselves. Alas!
That what has been heard is so shallow and limited as to reach this state—whether it be foolishness or madness, it is truly lamentable.
Yantou said: "In preaching the Dharma, one must be able to bring forth every word from within one's own breast to serve as a model for others.
It is simply because one is not deluded by the myriad objects before the senses and sounds that one knows the meaning within the scriptures."
There is also a path that ascends further, like clouds emerging from a high mountain or waterfalls gushing from a multitude of peaks—how truly marvelous!
The waters of a hundred rivers all ultimately return to the sea; when clouds emerge and their moisture flows forth to benefit the world, what joy could surpass this?

Thus, it becomes increasingly vast and increasingly empty, like waves and like the wind; not even a hair’s breadth can be grasped, nor is there the slightest obstruction, thereby manifesting the mind.
Drum Mountain said: "The twelve divisions of the teachings cannot sing it forth; ordinary beings and sages cannot encompass it; past and present cannot flow it."
Words and phrases cannot encompass it. The Tathāgata, with his spiritual wonders spanning a thousand ages, pours forth from within his breast that which is elegant, charming, and fresh;
it serves as both the ancient and the rule. At times it reveals the union of jade and璧 (bi), difficult to distinguish between paper and jade.

If one does not understand this, it becomes merely the circulation of worldly conventions. Yet, when this very sharp edge is applied directly, it is like the vast void where even a slender cloud is utterly non-existent.
The First Patriarch of Dongshan said: "To proclaim the vehicle of our school and expound the Great Teaching, one must possess a sharp and clear Dharma-eye;

only then can one discern the black from the white. This is because the true and the false share a single source; like water and milk in the same vessel, they are difficult to distinguish once they have reached this state."
Dongshan habitually used the eye within his mind to observe the forms outside his body; observing and observing again, he was able to distinguish the true from the false.
Now, as for those who are true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), they drive the oxen of the plowmen and snatch away the food of the hungry;

one must simply achieve the identity of mind and object, severing the eighth consciousness with a single stroke, so that the mind is free of leakage. Only then will there be a slight degree of resonance. Therefore, within the breast...
It is like swallowing and spitting out the Yangtze River; its skeletal structure is perfectly balanced, never failing to reveal itself throughout the entire body.
It flows freely, unbound by dharmas—how could one allow even the slightest trace of conditioned shadows to remain within the breast?

Master Linji said: "If you can realize that the myriad dharmas are unborn and that the mind is like an illusion or a transformation, such that not a single speck of dust or a single dharma remains, then everywhere is pure.
There is no Buddha and no sentient beings; there is no past and no present. When it is attained, it is attained."
There is no constraining of time or seasons, nor is there any cultivation or realization. There is neither gain nor loss; at all times, there is no other dharma whatsoever.
Even if there were a single dharma that transcended this, I would say it is like a dream or an illusion. Entering into all differentiated realms, it cannot be altered or exchanged.
It has never been separated from a single thought-moment; it is pure in every place. To claim, "I understand Chan, I understand the Way," is merely a flowery eloquence.
The river—all these are karmas that create the hells. If one is a true seeker of the Way, they do not perceive faults in the world;
they must urgently seek genuine insight. Only when one reaches the true mind and awakens to the perfect clarity of one's nature will it finally be completed.

As for the twelve divisions of the teachings, they are all expressions of symbolic manifestation. If students do not understand this, they simply follow the literal names and phrases of those manifestations.
The aforementioned understandings are all dependent and rely upon others; they fall within the realm of cause and effect and do not escape the birth and death of the triple world.
When the single thought-moment of the mind can attain mastery and liberation wherever one is, only then, having attained such understanding, can one truly begin to study the teachings.
The words of the Tathāgata are all correct speech. How could correct speech be subject to forced interpretation?

Whether manifesting skillful eloquence or revealing esoteric teachings, they possess a distinct character and spirit, utterly devoid of the scent of worldly toil or mundane flavor. His language transcends the dust of the world;
even as a hundred birds vie in song and the pine wind harmonizes with their melody, these all assist the Tathāgata’s discourse. I truly fear that by means of paper...
The pursuit of written characters through study consists entirely of conceptual discourse; it is not the Tathāgata’s true teaching. Thus, Master Yantou said:
"Within the great governing framework, one must recognize the phrase. If one does not recognize the phrase, it is difficult to engage in dialogue.
When there is no thought of anything at all, this is called the 'true phrase. Study is insufficient to peer into the source that has no beginning; words have no..."
One should contemplate so as to accord with the affairs of the age, exhausting and penetrating even the most subtle doubts, moving freely and spontaneously as one desires.
Only when a person possesses their own insight can they truly recognize the authentic purport within the Tathāgata’s teaching. The words of the Tathāgata are vibrant in every phrase;
every utterance is indeterminate, responding to conditions as needed, like an illusion or a transformation, like a pearl rolling across a tray—how could it be otherwise?
To grasp [the meaning] is to reveal the subtlety of the mind. People today fixate upon worldly words and letters to interpret the Tathāgata’s teachings;
how could they know that the Tathāgata’s words are not worldly words? How can one produce understanding merely by following the literal phrasing?
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Know that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind; thus one accomplishes wisdom."
The body does not awaken through another; therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "To uproot sentient beings from their various attachments.
When the Great Master Zhiwei reached this passage, he said, "This is true diligence; this is called the place of true Dharma-offering," and he attained a sudden, great awakening.
If one asks what principle the Great Master Zhiwei awakened to, only then will one know that the whole is but one.
The *svādhiṣṭhāna* (spontaneous empowerment) is without excavation, without mental application, without interruption, and without a place for deliberation.

How could one arbitrarily follow its words and phrases to excavate it? Therefore, regarding the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) taught in the scriptures—unimpededness in phenomena, unimpededness in principle, unimpededness in both phenomenon and principle—the reason why the principle of the "unimpededness of phenomena within phenomena" alone is difficult to awaken to is not because it is not the *Avataṃsaka*.
Once a sutra possesses these four kinds of unimpeded principles, all sutras are likewise so; this is the essential framework for the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.
Therefore, when the Great Master Zhiwei read the Lotus Sutra, he attained awakening, realizing that the entire earth is the Lotus Sutra.
The Great Master Yongming said: "Regarding all verbal designations, within the teachings of the Perfect School, they are all considered incomplete because the nature of words is detached from them;
this very detachment is liberation. To be deluded regarding the nature of all phenomena and to seek dharmas outside the mind is [to be unenlightened]."
For those who give rise to views based on words and letters, I now employ words and letters as an antidote to reveal the reality.

If one awakens to the source of all phenomena, one will no longer perceive even a hair’s breadth of the manifestation of words and letters. Only then does one know that all dharmas are the very nature of the mind;
thus, object and wisdom are interfused, and both form and emptiness are extinguished. At this moment of directly realizing perfect luminosity, one enters...
At this time of the equality of this single Dharma, what dharma is there that is a teaching to be abandoned? What dharma is there that is a patriarchal transmission to be revered?
What dharma is there that is sudden to be adopted? What dharma is there that is gradual to be rejected? Thus one knows that all are but the conceptual discriminations of the conscious mind.
Therefore, the patriarchs and Buddhas, through their skillful means, have extensively arrayed provisional gateways and fully prepared the vehicles of teaching. Only then...

He then attended the assembly; as soon as he attained the realization of his nature, he became immediately mindless. Both medicine and illness were simultaneously eliminated, and both teaching and contemplation came to rest (from the *Zongjing lu*).

Therefore, one must not cling to fixed doctrines of right and wrong when explaining the teachings. Speech possesses no inherent nature of right or wrong, nor does it harbor thoughts of right or wrong, nor does it engage in the discrimination of right or wrong.
Thus, that which speech issues forth from exists prior to the differentiation of right and wrong;
furthermore, there is no one who discriminates between right and wrong. This is precisely the Right Mindfulness of the Tathāgata, before sentient beings have undergone transformation.
This is the reality. It is the countenance of a thousand kalpas past. If one discriminates between speech and doctrine, right and wrong, or beauty and ugliness, then it is not the true countenance;
all such things are merely the conceptual calculations of the discriminating consciousness. Therefore, it is said: "Where there is only verbal expression, there is no real meaning at all."

The mind has neither reality nor delusion; reality and delusion arise from the conceptualizations of consciousness. Prior to the undifferentiated moment when a single thought arises through conditions, who is the Buddha?
Who is the mind? Who is the Dharma? It is only because of the swift functioning [of the mind] that one lacks the intention to discriminate and lacks the intention to form conditions;
yet every thought is the mind itself. One can only fail to sever the emotional fetters at the very first moment of seeing and hearing, leaving behind dry consciousness.

Waves surge upon the surface of love and hatred; the divine principle is easy to awaken to, yet habitual attachments are difficult to forget. When deluded, delusion arises; when awakened, delusion ceases.
Delusion has no source of delusion, and vertically there is no beginning. Since there is no beginning, how could there be an end?
Because the fundamental limit cannot be found, birth and death have no beginning. As the Great Master Linji said: "Following the current without ceasing, one asks about suchness..."

What? True illumination is boundless; it is described as being like something else. Free from characteristics and free from names, it is not received by the person. Having used the "blow-penetrating" sword, one must immediately polish it.
Principle must be suddenly awakened to; habituation must be gradually eliminated.
The Great Sage has appeared to awaken people, pointing directly to this light that has never changed or decayed for a thousand kalpas prior to this moment.
At all times, he handles the lump of clay; you must recognize it for yourself.
Do not allow yourself to drown in paper, ink, and written words. Once separated from these words, it is no less than a monkey losing its tree—there will be nowhere left to rest.

One establishes one’s destiny therein. Yet, those who do not realize that what cannot be contained within words lies beyond the physical form—wherein liver and gall are laid bare, surging and galloping in every direction, releasing and gathering as they go—remain in a state where things subtly reflect one another.
They merely converse with worldly people about worldly dharmas, no longer knowing that there exists a matter that transcends them. In this traceless realm, one may examine it.

Indeed, there is a place where the mind-consciousness is absent that can be recognized; thus, the Way of the *qin* is honored. Its roots lie in ancient sounds, and one may briefly glimpse the origins of its resonance and instruments.

As for the techniques of the fingers, the rhythms of the notes, and the subtlety of their harmonization, they do not deviate from what is correct, yet they awaken the human heart across ten thousand generations.

It is as if one were about to seize the void itself; grasping the brush, one sweeps across it with bold strokes, both horizontal and vertical, marvelous and intricate, harmonizing with the great sages of a thousand ages.
Like an aged steed tethered to its stall, his spirit overflows; like a crane piercing the clouds, his gaze reaches ten thousand *li* without obstruction.

One then perceives the celestial mechanism suddenly stirred, revealing the hands and eyes of one’s entire being. Long ago, Gongming Xuan studied under Zengzi for three years without reading a single book.
Zengzi said, "Xuancheng, you have lived at my gate for three years; why have you not studied? Gongming Xuancheng replied, "How would I dare not study?
When I saw you, Master, in the palace courtyard with your parents present, the sound of your voice never reached even the dogs or horses—this was what I studied, yet I was unable to master it.
I saw you, Master, when receiving guests: you were so respectful and frugal."

"I have not been indolent. I have proclaimed my studies, yet I have not mastered them. I have proclaimed my views upon seeing you, Master, and while dwelling in the court under your solemn supervision, I have not brought disgrace upon myself. I have proclaimed my studies, yet I have not mastered them.
Having proclaimed these three things, and having studied yet not mastered them, how would I dare not study while dwelling at your gate, Master? Zengzi rose from his mat and apologized for him.
It is said: "Zhang San did not equal [the clarity of] Xuancheng; he merely mastered his studies.
*Lengyan Jijie Ming* (The Illumination of Beating the Beat of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra), composed by the śramaṇa Dashao.
Recorded by the disciple Zhiri:

A student who studies the Way must attain realization for themselves and overturn [delusion] to its very depths. How could they merely consume the wild fox drool from the lips and corners of others' mouths?
On another day, all such people will be nothing more than those begging iron staffs from the Old Lord Yama; what use would that be?
In engaging in dialogue, you must emerge from the place of your own true investigation and genuine realization.
Only then will you be able to cast all of Śākyamuni’s wild fox spittle and saliva entirely into the great ocean of the eastern seas, leaving no trace behind.
Vomiting it forth from your own breast, there shall be no stagnation; like a pearl rolling upon a tray, it leaves no shadow.
His traces galloped through the contemporary world; as his divine gaze turned upon himself, there was nothing of its subtle essence that he did not penetrate.

He gathered it within the tip of a hair and released it to pervade the six directions. Within the midst of written characters, one must discern the Eye of the Tathāgata, whose radiance shines everywhere.
There is not a single word that does not reveal the entire being of the World-Honored One;
there is not a single character that is not the place where Śākyamuni the Old Man lost his very life.

It is simply because one’s lifelong study has not been refined enough to discern and penetrate the root of birth and death, thereby manifesting that state of reality prior to the birth of one's parents. People...

Each person claims to hold the pearl of the mystical serpent; every household claims to embrace the jade of Mount Jing. Yet they remain茫然 (máng rán—bewildered and lost), unable to reflect things as they truly are.

With nothing hidden and no path to follow, they cannot penetrate the subtle and profound to investigate ultimate reality. In seeing, there is neither delusion nor enlightenment; in the mind’s vision, there is no division.
There is nothing they do not know to exist, yet their verbal expressions appear brilliant only like the surface of water, drifting aimlessly.
It is said that when one is vast and boundless, the literary expression arises spontaneously; this is because the principle transcends language and written characters.
That the noble lineage radiates its brilliance and that eloquence flows like a cascading river—is this not the light of true insight, the primordial and pure essence of Nirvana?
Those who study today are unable to walk in accordance with the Way and roam within their own nature, nor can they ride upon the Buddha-principle to govern their minds. The Path...
The eye is not yet clear; though the mundane and supramundane are constantly manifest before one, one cannot discern them, remaining instead as a "spiritual bone" for a thousand ages.
Only when the root of birth and death is pierced through does one realize that the true medicine is present before one. As for "being unable to discern": it refers to this very state.

The vital energy is clear and the spirit is lucid; his talent and refined elegance are as if dwelling within the Great Void, floating aloft while manifesting the profound winds of a thousand ages to respond to the world.
With his spirit harmonized and his very bones suffused with grace, he must realize this truth, so that he regards a thousand or ten thousand generations as a single day.
Pure within and integrated without, he remains untainted by the mundane world.

It is obstructed by language and written characters; therefore, by extensively gathering the subtle and refined and molding the wondrous meanings, one accords with the intent of the Tathāgata without expending even a fraction of effort, enabling students to analyze principles and open their spirits.
Discarding the refined essence, even a single phrase from a thousand autumns—this ocean of the Dharma-voice—is not the true vision of the Buddhas;

who could grant such [a realization]? One who has never known its pure and void substance, whose bare bones are inherently spiritual and cannot be defiled, will find that when not a single word is forced, the mirror of the mind becomes ever more luminous.
Its resonance is like metal and stone; all arises from the very spirit of one’s own character.
It is revealed that wondrous discernment, whether expansive or subtle, does not flow from anything other than the ocean of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
Therefore, there is nothing the mind can conceal; what we humans cannot conceal within our own minds is precisely this.

For this reason, it is difficult to distinguish between the mind and its perceptions. Yet, in the world, there is no mind capable of concealing itself, nor is there any perception capable of concealing itself.
That which the mind reveals yet one cannot know for oneself—this indicates that one has not yet been able to know the mind.
When the obscured and ignorant attain illumination through the radiance of light, who could claim to see it in its full revelation? One need only speak directly of its ultimate destination.
Only by exhausting the source of the myriad phenomena and discerning the functions of the thousand spirits can one illuminate true vision. How can you say otherwise?

This is to expound the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama. Therefore, by pruning away flowery rhetoric and expanding upon the ultimate Way, I have set forth its grand framework, tracing it from its origin to its conclusion to capture its true essence. Do not seek after the branches and leaves;

rather, let it be like the flow of the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers, where all doubts are suddenly dissolved like melting ice. Only one who possesses the beauty of Nanwei can be discussed as a virtuous lady.
The sharpness of the Dragon Abyss may then be deliberated upon for cutting and severing.

To propagate its essential meaning, one must sift through the myriad words to reveal what previous masters had not yet disclosed and to pour forth the true marrow of the Tathāgata; this shall serve as a supplement for the future, though it cannot be fully detailed here.
Formerly, Wang Dun asked Chan Master Juefan about the prophetic utterances of Bao Gong, which number in the thousands and hundreds.
"A year passes as if it were a single day. By what path does one arrive at this? Juefan said, "When clarity and purity reside within the person, their will and spirit are like those of a deity.
When something is about to arrive, its omens must first appear. These are the words of Confucius. Is it not all a matter of 'inverted thinking'?
If inverted thinking is extinguished, one will see through the three periods of time. How could Master Baohua have had inverted thinking? Dunsu clapped his hands and laughed."
He said: "How excellent is this discourse! Yet, is there truly a path for overturning deluded perceptions?
The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa is the very fruit-body of all Buddhas; it reverses the decline of this degenerate age and sustains the life-force of wisdom for all sentient beings."
There is neither past nor present; may it not differ from the true source. Whether as mind or as function, it has never failed to manifest in the form of the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*).

All sentient beings cannot analyze the vision of the Tathāgata, nor can they know the crown of the Tathāgata, yet [the Buddha] thereby reveals the divine power and function of all Buddhas. He employs the speech of sentient beings; thus, he is a sentient being.
This is the dharma-gate of self-enjoyment; it is the place where one establishes one's body and sustains one's life.
The World-Honored One has pointed out the eye of all Buddhas and emitted the light from the crown of his head.
The wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*—as this single word "wondrous" is uttered, it grinds together with worldly flavors;
common speech and common conduct, along with good and evil, right and wrong, are melted into a single mass and blended into one lump.
It overturns the lair of principle and upends the realm of emotion—spontaneously so.
The true destination is spontaneously and divinely transformed, requiring no artificial carving or polishing. Though existing in the world, it is not altered by the world;
though transcending the world, it cannot be fully assimilated by the world. Because its true purity remains unfragmented, it constitutes the fundamental, primordially pure essence of *nirvāṇa*.
This is the original source of all Buddhas. It flows without dispersing and functions without dividing. Therefore, the World-Honored One—
Throughout the forty-nine years of its total functioning, that which has never been distracted is the single wondrous syllable;
because it is without cognition, it is called *śamatha*, and because it is without ignorance, it is called *samādhi*.

In the *dhyāna* of the three correct contemplations, it is called "stopping by realizing the reality" (*tǐzhēn zhǐ*), because consciousness has not yet moved; it is called "stopping through skillful means according with conditions" (*suíyuán fāngbiàn zhǐ*), because it is inconceivable;
and it is called "stopping without clinging to the two extremes" (*bùzhuò èbiān zhǐ*).

This is, moreover, the fruit-body (*guǒtǐ*) in which the original source has not yet dispersed—the primordial state where the simple and the refined have not yet been differentiated. The World-Honored One, wishing to [liberate] all sentient beings throughout the great earth...
All are, moreover, the substance of the true origin. If they are invaded by the functioning of consciousness, the sagely virtue becomes obscured and the substance of primordial luminosity is lost.
That which is not the triple world is divided into the triple world; that which has no past or present is distinguished into past and present.
There are no sentient beings, yet the appearance of sentient beings is established. These Buddhas have thus become sentient beings.
All the Buddhas throughout the entire earth are, at this very moment, manifesting the forms of wriggling insects and sentient creatures.
One’s own single point of true essence has been hollowed out and exhausted; it will be difficult for a Great Sage to emerge and save us.
Were it not for a Great Sage, one could not restore their true nature, extinguish their consciousness, and perfect their essence.
I fear that among the people of the world, there may not be a single person capable of perfecting their mind;
nor is there a single person capable of fully realizing the essential body of all Buddhas, restoring the original source, and entering the Great Samādhi. Having already realized this...

This is Nirvana; it is the state where consciousness has already been extinguished. Therefore, when the Great Sages appeared in the world, they never allowed their own minds to be invaded by consciousness.
For this reason, Xu You hid among the reeds, Lao Dan maintained the center, Fuxi drew the hexagrams, and King Wen fully revealed the *I Ching*.
That the sages and philosophers were so busily occupied, while the Old Man of Lu (Confucius) acted as a mender, was because of the world.
The Venerable One employs the art of illusory transformation to awaken all people in the world.

Thus, when all sentient beings realize their own minds, they will finally know that their own minds are entirely illusory transformations, and that these illusory transformations are themselves their own minds.

Therefore, it harmonizes the myriad dharmas within a single wondrousness and encompasses the minds of all sentient beings throughout the great earth, causing them all to enter into *śamatha* and *dhyāna*.

Thus, there is not a single moment when any sentient being in the entire world has not been analyzing *samādhi* and *dhyāna*, fusing true insight (*samyag-darśana*), and integrating the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*). How could they ever have remained silent?
The Initial Expedient Means of Gathering.
The World-Honored One directly grasps the samādhi of the daily activities of sentient beings and melts it within śamatha;
by means of samāpatti-dhyāna, he dissolves it into the initial expedient means of gathering. This may be applied as a mundane dharma, and it may also be applied as a supramundane dharma.
It is also so. Melted into a single mass and blended into one lump, it cannot be distinguished and cannot be conceptualized.
When it is brought forth, there is not yet a trace of chewing upon it;

even the Elder Śākyamuni could not employ even a hair’s breadth of skillful means, nor could he employ even a hair’s breadth of thought or deliberation. At the very moment that the initial thought was first aroused, each...
Each person must examine themselves: can you still recognize the countenance that existed ten thousand kalpas ago?

If you can recognize this very mind-moment of discernment as it emerges in every thought, and thereby recognize this state of luminosity prior to the birth of your parents, then all the many stinking, rotten entanglements of Śākyamuni will be seen through.
Not even a single hair’s breadth of effort is required, nor can one display even a hair’s breadth of skillful artifice.

How could one know that a single thought-moment can realize that all sentient beings throughout the great earth shall all attain Buddhahood? How could one know that the manifestations of the Buddhas of the three periods of time are fully revealed within the single thought-moment of sentient beings?
Its form is hidden yet capable of manifestation; its sound is revealed yet eternally concealed. By means of this—
An extraordinary person is able to perceive an extraordinary form. Possessing extraordinary eyes, they do not emerge from a state of forgetful thought;
rather, they take up that which has never yet been bitten or chewed.
Before even being born of parents, they cast it before others, desiring only that all people likewise shall not bite or wound it, but instead personally employ it to sever [delusion].
In a person’s divination and deliberation, one cuts off the seeds from before the beginningless kalpas of humanity.

Under direct speech, not even a hair’s breadth of conjecture or deliberation remains. One releases one’s own radiance, illuminating heaven and earth, flashing like lightning and startling with thunder.
What else exists within heaven and earth that could possibly reach such a state?
Thus, even the Elder Śākyamuni could not employ even a hair’s breadth of artifice. This natural, true essence is how the mind manifests through the spirit;
it arises before consciousness has moved. Therefore, one employs the non-conscious mind to act in the realm of the non-phenomenal.
It is the realm of contemplation; therefore, it cannot be invaded by the movement of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
It is said that where speech is without stagnating thought, the mind possesses the consciousness capable of transformation. When consciousness moves, the Truth (*tathatā*) is abandoned;

when the mind is luminous yet obstructed, limitations arise. Through luminosity there is knowledge, and through that, delusion (*moha*) is produced; thus, the essence of primordial luminosity is lost. Therefore—
It is said that those who use [the mind] all day long without knowing it fall into the various realms of existence.
Therefore, the true mind cannot be employed in the world, nor can it discern worldly affairs.
To clarify what is not clear and to know what is not known—those who can thus know the world do so not through the reality of the mind. When right and wrong are made manifest, the Way...
This is what has caused such deficiency. That which emerges from Heaven and Earth is that which even the most brilliant insights and ultimate principles cannot reach.

It is only because we know that what people speak directly cannot be grasped as the mind, nor can it be taken as the Way through mere clarity, that Śākyamuni’s transformative influence upon beings was exercised solely by means of shifting his words for practical application.
Observing only the transformations of words as the Tathāgata’s unimpeded eloquence is what constitutes the Dharma.
While it exhausts the minds of all people in the world, there is no function that can fully encompass it;

and while it exhausts the mechanisms of the Tathāgata’s transformations, for this reason, throughout forty-nine years, the World-Honored One never spoke a single word from among his own dharmas of self-enjoyment.
He transformed and guided sentient beings for forty-nine years, yet he never gave a single dharma to anyone;

he did nothing but speak directly of their ultimate destination. This "pulse of speech"—this one essential secret that constitutes the life-force of the Tathāgata transmitted by Bodhidharma—is as precarious as a dangling thread.
The World-Honored One never failed to reveal it completely. It lies within...

At the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he is called the one who speaks as it is, the one who speaks truthfully, the one who speaks authentically, the one who does not speak deceptively, and the one who does not speak otherwise.
At the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he utters three times words of sincere truth;

amidst more than sixty thousand words, at the very conclusion, he correctly proclaims that he transmits and upholds the Buddha’s words, which are solely direct speech, serving as the teacher for ten thousand generations.
This can only belong to the Great Sage. There is no meaning within the written word by which it can be expressed.
Therefore, even when exhausting all words for the myriad things, one cannot speak with directness.
When speech is not direct, it is invaded by conceptual cognition; thus, one cannot settle the minds of the myriad things as true, nor can one fathom them.
To take the hearts of things as the basis for teaching is to be unable to harmonize the hearts of the myriad things and abide in the realm of no-thought;
it is to be unable to transform the mechanisms of the myriad things so that they each return to the state prior to the birth of their parents.
Transforming firewood to brew tea upon a single blade of thatch;
the crimson flames of heaven burn eternally amidst ten thousand fingers. The conditions for this Dharma-offering arose by chance;
the Xiao Stream was boiled into coolness, yet all became furnaces and bellows. Within the cauldrons and furnaces of the boiling oil, who will reach out a hand?
To hold it aloft amidst fierce flames—what need is there to bring firewood to the blaze? Let sandalwood be brought piece by piece;
what harm is there in that? Let the jade trees stand in dense rows; why begrudge plucking out branch after branch? Hack the azure, split the emerald; cut through the jade, cleave the gold.
Carrying the full load back, everything that falls is no longer another's thing; moving freely within the realm, one masters the art of reaping the very last blade.
This single point of light from a lamp of transformation illuminates the three thousand worlds, piercing straight through the dark paths of the Dharma-realm to the inner court of Maitreya.

Constantly radiant, it resembles the opening of the Palace of Broad Cold (the Moon Palace), reflecting a thousand layers of jeweled nets; like the bright sun suspended in the sky, it sends forth ten thousand paths of golden serpents.
Touching the white tuft of hair between the brows, everything becomes the color of jade; illuminating the marks of the Dharma-body, the entire earth turns to gold.
Every object emits its own brilliance, and every atom interpenetrates one another. Alas! Do not say that light does not arise from this very place.
All this has been obtained through the kindling of the flame; almsgiving has already been bestowed. Continue this illumination, bringing forth even a little, lest it remain perpetually obscured.
Expel the insects.

Sentient beings and Buddhas share the same source; their nature is without high or low. The Dharma-body manifests mutually, yet the retributive bodies have their rises and falls. Forms are divided into ten thousand categories, and essences are arrayed in a thousand ways.
Comets and meteors appear within the subtle celestial sphere, and portents of calamity manifest in the land of Wu. It is now the season of late summer.

When stones are scorched and metal flows, it is the season when the myriad things flourish and thrive, and when pines and bamboos shed their verdant hues; those of fragile constitution are thus aligned with this natural order.

Floating blossoms vie for splendor; hidden forms possess haughty bones. There stands the mark of a deep green, pure substance—lofty trees standing in dense array amidst the weeds of a profusion of myriad flowers.
The incantations of demonic karma push, carve, and strip away; they gnaw and devour, soften and wound.
The myriad fragrant blossoms have fallen away, all yielding their splendor to the natural order; they stand in dense, withered decay, yet only the solitary, lofty trunk remains upright.

Having encountered this desolation and decline, they rest in a state of withered exhaustion. The Way of the heavenly seasons is discordant, and the suitability of the earthly terrain is damaged and destroyed.
Being unable to achieve harmony, calamity and transgression descend. We humbly pray that you may realize the nature of dharmas as being like that which is bent and curved.
Manifesting samādhi as if biting or sucking; casting off the coarse form, spiritual powers become wondrous of themselves. Shedding the burdens of karma, one transcends to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Furthermore, it causes pines and bamboos to retain their verdancy, and flowers and trees to be fragrant;
it causes orchids to grow again to display their elegance, and causes trunks to stand firm while sprouts emerge.

In offering this memorial for my parents, how could I know that my own body is like a drifting duckweed? My life is as fragile as a blade of grass; as my form undergoes transformation with all things, I am struck by the vast expanse of the ocean of karma.
Yet the mind remains truly eternal, and I am startled by the distant and desolate nature of the perilous path. Alas! The Dharma-nature is empty and numinous; I lament the debt of parental kindness.
Boundless is our debt of gratitude. As the realms of light and darkness are separated by profound obscurity, I lament how the Way of my son may be furthered.

Were it not for the vast compassion of our Buddha, how could the lingering soul within the netherworld be guided? Alas! I cast myself with sincerity before the Buddhist monastery and communicate my earnest devotion to the Awakened Heaven.

Whatever transgressions I have committed through shame or remorse, I entrust them all to the pity of your compassionate mercy. Welcome, O Son of the Buddha; you shall truly fulfill this pure intention. As dust falls away into emptiness, so shall my karmic burdens vanish.

Rightly contemplating the ultimate reality (paramārtha), one perceives that thought is identical to empty space. Deeply entering the wondrous samādhi, there is no conflict between movement and stillness.
Seated in quietude within the water-moon dharma-assembly, uninterrupted by morning or evening, one accomplishes the Buddha-work of empty flowers.
The Miaozong of Zifusi Temple has burned this Miaozong.
This Miaozong was always upon the tip of a single hair, emitting great radiance; from within the eye of a skull, it illuminated heaven and earth.
Today, having left behind his private possessions, he is now in the hands of this mountain monk. This "hawk-stink" robe—its grease...

Anointing his cap with oil, he entered the *Samādhi of the Fiery Light* before the assembly of humans and devas. He ignited a blazing, crimson flame that reached the heavens, releasing the true fire of the emptiness of nature.
He drove away the hornless iron ox, leaped forth with the roar of a golden-maned lion, and struck down the peak of Mount Bian.
He terrified Sumeru until it fled in retreat; the pine winds became utterly frantic, and all the forest trees were completely [overturned].
A roar! A hundred birds wail in sorrow as the mountains and rivers shed tears. In the end, where will one find a place to settle?
(He draws a circle and says: Yet it is right here that one hides one's roots and avoids one's ugliness. (He gives a shout: The Elephant King has cast off his golden tether;
soaring upward, he rushes straight into the clouds.
Together with Xing’an of Lengyan Temple, we performed the cremation;
from the beginning, he did not recognize his own natural nose. Today, it is fully revealed and exposed. With his whole body, he leaps into the great void.
His two eyes are as clear and piercing as lightning. For over sixty years, he failed to seek it out; in a single morning, the clouds disperse and the wind [blows].
Previously distinct; now the fierce dragon has fled, leaving only the new single horn. Transverse and longitudinal throughout the Dharma-realm, wild and decisive.
The jade pillar gathers clouds; the Tiāoxī stream cuts through. But tell me, where exactly does the Venerable Xing’ān establish his dwelling?
(He draws a circle and says: Last night the jade qílín fled; turning its body, it leapt out from the golden cave.
Recorded by the Disciple Chi from the Thousand Pines Notes:
A Eulogy on the Maitreya Image.
This rogue! Without a shred of dignity, he constantly haunts the streets, accustomed to begging. With a massive belly that holds nothing but filth and stench, even the inner court cannot contain him;
his place is surely in hell. (Eh! It would be as if one were to dye the void with black ink.
They go straight into hell like a shot arrow.
This Guanyin image is a wild fox spirit; she puts on such a foolish appearance. Who painted this? To reveal such an ugly form!
All day long you deceive sentient beings while prostrating before an image of Avalokiteśvara. If you were to see him again, he would severely rebuke you with thirty blows of the staff.
You are the fellow whose jaw was broken by the image of Bodhidharma; you are a man who cannot be cured even by medicine. The Western Land cannot contain you; come to this Eastern Land.
"What business brings you here? You are accustomed to deceiving others with the belongings of another, yet you yourself do not possess even a hair’s breadth of anything rare.
If you happen to run into me, you will have no mercy; I shall strike you across the back and return the staff to him."
A Puxian Praising Another Puxian Riding an Elephant: Two by two, they are distinct and each is unique. Puxian rides the elephant, and the elephant carries the man;
Yet the nostrils have always been one and the same. If you can examine this with clarity, Each and every one must also possess the three.
The Tenth Staff:
Inscribed upon the staff is the legacy of the ancestral master Zhongfeng of Lengyan Temple;

its bamboo joints are bound in a spiral pattern where colored clouds once gathered. When the sun sets, the mountain seems to clasp its peak, revealing the traces of dew. It may still bear the marks of sudden snow and rain.
A bamboo hat; only when lightning and thunder strike swiftly does one truly know you. Your remaining livelihood is the pair of Tianmu Peaks;
your entire being is the flowery elegance of five-colored clouds. Only these traces of a hundred years remain; who would feel such sorrow as to cease their earnest devotion?

When the Master of the Secret Treasury left his hat behind, it was as if the weather were about to clear; he protected the spiral patterns of his shell-like hair, fearing that the divine light might reveal the traces of his bare head. No longer dwelling in his native land, he remained hidden beyond the world;

though his physical remains have vanished, his traces remain solemnly present. Only his full moon-like face survives for us to gaze upon today; had he not possessed this perfect halo, who would have known him?
Seen and heard: A rain of flowers falls upon a single niche; the mountain temple trembles. Where has the Master’s body not been scattered?
He draws lotuses from the channel, unaware of cold or heat, unaware of autumn. Having exhausted all worldly ties, he still finds no rest. A wild goose cries out once across the heavens.
Falling. Only when the mountain stream flows can one see that there is no water.

Together with the painter, Layman Chen, you have sketched out the very bones of the mountains and rivers; yet can you still write from your own mind? Try looking at the places where the brushstrokes gallop; you must recognize the truth within the tip of the pen.

The Song of the Twelve Hours: Dawn, the Hour of the Tiger (Tiyin). The two eyes are opened wide and see clearly for themselves. At this time, all is silent and still; From of old, no guest has ever reached the wattle gate.
Stretching out his two feet, he is as lively as a qilin; Trampling through empty space, where could there be any dust? Looking at one another, the monkeys...

A bird passes by at dawn; it laughs that my mountain dwelling is utterly without neighbor. At the rising of the sun in the hour of Mao, illumination and function are simultaneous, with nothing left unclarified.
The golden crow faces us directly, without concealment; mountains, rivers, and the great earth are ever radiant and bright. The clay ox bellows; the stone tiger roars.
At the sea gate, waves strike as the red wheel [of the sun] grows small. The leviathans swallow up the peaks of Mount Sumeru. I ask you practitioners: how many [have seen this]?
I understand. At the hour of eating, I know for myself whether the water and gruel are cold or hot; coarse food is accepted as it comes, according to my lot.
As the years have passed, old age has come, and poverty is complete. Sometimes I spit it out, sometimes I swallow it;

coming and going, such a person as I has never heard the music of the second meal. In the end, all is worn away, fittingly like Chu or Qin. At the hour of Youzhong (the fifth watch), white clouds laugh at me.
Without fame or profit, one finds joy in the empty mountains, forgetting both silence and clamor. At this time, there is the sound of birds, lovely and verdant.
Do not reflect; do not deliberate. One who knows the sound is not encountered by chance. Upon meeting him, you fail to recognize him. Life and death, when viewed thus, are truly objects of laughter.
At noon in the south, a monkey hangs from a wall, able to climb and dance. Letting go of the hand on the precipice—this is a true master.
Now, the great earth has never possessed so much as an inch of soil. Whether walking or sitting, look repeatedly toward the east, west, south, and north.

A brilliant red light blazes fiercely throughout one’s entire body; take heed, O people of this age, and do not be reckless! Before the sun has turned its course, the fisherman chants his song as he departs by the riverbank.
Holding aloft a fierce dragon, he will surely cook it alive. Whatever is picked up at hand is nothing but this—splash!
Heavenly wind. Do not be startled or afraid. Cast open the nets that envelop heaven and earth; those who understand this with ease find their own benefit.
This shall prevent drifting dust from chasing idle vapors. At the hour of Shen (5–7 p.m.): Forest winds roar and thunder across the universe.
A single raindrop from the south divides the rainbow; light clouds to the north encircle the sun’s orb. The riverbanks split; the tides divide. The evening rain falls in a drizzling mist.
Arriving at the ferry crossing, look upon the white-haired one whose body is like a crane; washing his feet in the pine wind, he passes through the world as a traveler.

At the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), the fleeting light of time rushes by like lightning. Day by day, month by month, how much more can there be? One must ensure that at all times there is neither grasping nor rejecting.
Wild birds return home; the wind rises in the bamboo. Amidst the shade of the forest, there is nothing to do but lean alone. Observe this freedom throughout the twelve hours of the day.
Body. A clay ox bellows under the moon amidst the western wind. At the hour of dusk, the great earth is vast and dark as lacquer.
To abandon darkness for light is not yet true; why needlessly waste words on light and darkness?

There is no person, nor is there a Buddha. From within my own mouth I blow the flute: in the blazing heat of the sixth month, snow falls in profusion. On the peak of Mount Bian, one laughs without end. Man.
The hour of Hai (11 p.m.): Sleep is deep and the mind is dark; who is the master? The pillow laughs *he-he* within the dream, yet it is but a gourd that cannot form a team.
The dew is thick and the moon sinks into the sea; the solitary wild goose utters its cawing cry.
If you can recognize this very sound, the stone man sits at night as Avalokiteśvara. The hour of Zi (midnight): Mountains and rivers vanish; the Master of Masters.
The wind blows at the corner of the roof, yet no one knows; one sleeps in a thatched hut amidst a mound of mud. The moon is ever full, the clouds are rushing by;
a stone woman conceives, a cow gives birth to a foal. By day one eats in hunger, by night one sleeps; the Son of Heaven of the imperial house is like a sieve.
At the hour of the Rooster (1–3 a.m.), having awakened on the road, one startles the sleeping dog. The flow of the spring pours forth the melody of autumn sounds; the clouds deepen.
The secluded path is walked by no one; the light of dew reveals the beautiful and the ugly. Upon this mass of bare flesh, hands move freely in every direction.
The myriad phenomena of the forested world are all in turmoil, yet from the beginning, the great earth has never accepted them.
On New Year’s Eve, the branch of Tianmu from Yangwu rushes straight toward the east. The mountains wind and turn with a majestic and vast power.

They coil and twist for thousands of li, with layered emerald peaks and tens of thousands of ridges. To the north, Lake Gusu drenches the sky in azure; the Yangtze River serves as its girdle and sash.

Winding along, the ridges and peaks stand out in exquisite beauty, veiled only by curtains of rosy clouds; their jagged crags bare their summits as they pierce the mists. Several peaks coil around to form Yang Valley;

hanging cliffs and steep precipices gaze down from the mountain tops. Towering and majestic, they stand like jade pillars with the force of a screen, bowing in toward the constellation of Kui to form an outer protection.
Cascading springs flow directly downward with a gurgling sound; spraying snow and flying crystals resemble white egrets. The monastic quarters...
Cloud vapors connect to the Eaves of the Ancestral Hall; at the mountain peaks, sun and moon alternate in swallowing and spitting them out.

Azure mists veil and reflect the emerald lapis lazuli; upon the brows of the banks, countless monks stand amidst the falling snow. Clear pearls pool in the marshes where dragons and serpents dwell; before the cliffs, strange rocks resemble fierce tigers.
The sound of bells and chimes drifts from afar, mingling with the cries of wild monkeys as they leap over the ridges. In the gullies and ravines, the rustling of leaves continues through the night.
Long have the pines stood, their winds rustling and howling day after day. From time to time, a cowherd comes with his "kuan-nai" chant;
sometimes I stand face-to-face with a woodcutter, our voices rising in unison. I have taken temporary refuge beneath the western crags, and by chance have stayed here for these thirty nights.

Not a single thing has passed through the new year; once the meal of pickled vegetables and *kaṇṭhaka* garlands has satisfied my hunger, I burn the remaining jade-like branches of the snow-laden pine. The tender buds first...
Cooking before the flowers have been released; it is not said that in old age one lacks many inspirations.

Joyfully meeting this auspicious evening amidst the mist and clouds, I chant of the West, knowing neither East nor West. Whatever is brought forth, every dharma is entirely equal. Where the colored clouds pass, they divide the pines.
The shadow: the crimson sun devours the waves as it sinks low; the blue lotus tongue manifests the form of Amitābha; the white jade brow-hair divides to reveal the brandishing of the precious sword.
In an instant, Nāsatya’s eyes are revealed—who then is life-and-death, and who is delusion?
In my first year of life, the Wood-Dragon year, I entered this world in profound stillness, as if in a dream. Upside-down and crosswise, I have been driven along by the currents of the age.

For sixty years I have hurried about in a frantic rush, bearing the heavy burden of this skin-sack upon my two shoulders. How could I have known that beneath my feet there was a colt, so elegant and capable, to carry me back home?
In flight and motion; as my horse-teeth grow, my countenance gradually declines. With snow filling my head, my body is of no use; I am now old and can only pity myself.
My limbs are so clumsy that my head is constantly in pain. Gathering ink, I find it difficult to write the Eightfold Script;
picking up my staff, I have lost the ability to wield it. There is no way to reach the Western Paradise; let the donkey’s womb and the horse’s belly send me there.
Moreover, I am now old, my hair like snow; thought after thought, the dust-mind flows on, unextinguished. Constantly I stretch forth my mother-born hands;

the spring breeze smiles, breaking open the empty void of my mouth. On this auspicious night, the bright moon shines in the azure vastness of space; letting go of all concerns within the boundless expanse.
Rest and relax. In leisure, read the *Anakṣara-sūtra*; when weary, go to your pillow—this is the true wondrous method. A human life in this world is but a short time;
I am fortunate that my life’s work is now complete. Do not regard the mundane world as a great age; even the Buddhas and patriarchs would consider it but a speck in their eyes.
On this New Year’s morning, everyone says a year has been added; yet in our Way, one year has now been subtracted. Increase and decrease, coming and going, have no fixed measure;
only by being able to exhaust all worldly conditions can one truly know the Master within those conditions, remaining constant through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
It is so. Without increase or decrease, how could there be a path? Why need a single word be transmitted by mouth?
Behold the four stanzas on plum blossoms:

ten thousand points of azure mountain color, half-green; the shadows of a thousand peaks fall upon the central courtyard. Only when one perceives the spring breeze through the curtain does one truly know it.
Movement: The plum blossoms on the full branches have all released their fragrance.
A single branch, its scent staining the summit of the solitary peak, its tender buds vying to bloom amidst the snow. Through the empty window, the white spirit of the flower enters;
with a face full of spring wind, it smiles as I arrive.
Reluctantly she withholds her bashful bloom from opening upon the ridge; she hides her form to reflect her蛾眉 (arched brows) within the shadows. Behold her face, full of springtime charm and grace;
her bone-chillingly pure skin reveals no hidden intent (the plum beneath the water).
Jade embroidery adorns the thousand peaks, resembling auspicious snow; its fragrant scent is first perceived as that of cold plum blossoms. It veils the colored brush, reflecting only pure white;
even as the herons fly, they still carry the spring back with them.

While walking on the mountain path, he laughs and points to the mountain peak where no summit is revealed. Where white clouds drift, the tracks of foxes are cut off. Raising his head, he sees a wild goose passing by;
it pierces through tens of thousands of layers of cloud-covered mountains.

Upon reaching the mountain stream, the moon is at its purest white; my straw sandals tread upon the azure depths of the great void. My staff rests across my shoulder as the stars and constellations shine bright;
deep in the night, the sword emits a crimson glow. The wind’s breath is evenly divided among the mists and clouds;
colorful vapors deeply shroud the moss-covered rocks. Looking up and down across heaven and earth, my Way is vast and spacious; the cry of wild geese awakens the traveler from the world of men.

Wandering on foot amidst illness, a single umbrella flutters as he roams the lakes and seas. Like a solitary cloud or a wild crane, who could detain him? Since ancient times, such has been the way of the wandering monk;

only by exhausting every ounce of spirit does one find rest. Only when the straw sandals are worn through does one reach the bottom; only when the clouds and mist are swept away is the truth revealed.
With eyes fully open, he commands his own awakening as a thousand rainbows snap; in a moment of laughter, he first perceives the autumn of the Five Peaks.
Rain falls in profusion upon the green moss, and fragments of evening glow reflect through the window. Before the steps, the bamboo turns a deep azure amidst the clouds;
outside the courtyard, a light breeze rolls back the mist. Alas, when shall my worldly ties end? For now, I shall dwell at ease within these mountain ravines.
Forget all worldly concerns. Should the day come when you ride the phoenix away, you will laughingly point at the void and strike the thunder.

Seeing off the Chief Administrator on his eastern journey, the emerald waters of the Tiexi River flow wide and full in spring. The Master rows his boat toward the east; the green mountains on both banks follow him.
Departing for the headlands where egrets break the waves at Bai Lu Island, the boat travels upon the Xiao River;
the waters fill the stream-heads and the moon fills the currents. There is not a single fish or dragon that does not swallow it down. One has just encountered the three tiers of Yu’s steps.
Waves! They spew forth radiance ten thousand miles across the autumn sky.
This "Words on Herding Oxen" says:
this ox has a powerful and sturdy body; how many people can understand how to lead or ride it? For the sake of greed, it chases the tender green grass upon the embankment.

Fence by fence, they do nothing but seek the fragrant and pursue the verdant; rushing forward, they do not look back at the impending peril. Who would have known that the mountains are distant and the paths secluded?
Turning their heads, they find it late to reach home. Now the cowherd has a purpose: he carefully binds them with the tether and holds the nose-rope high.
Entering the mud, entering the water—ultimately, he will not follow you. Do not let him go to swagger along the long embankment;
lest he suddenly startle up ten-thousand-li clouds in flight, or fearfully trample through a thousand-qi of glass-like waves, returning once more to roar through the great void.

Walking through the snow, heaven and earth already reveal their true forms; how can one speak of lightness when the falling snow has not yet ceased? Standing tall among a thousand peaks, who can truly perceive them?
Ten thousand points of azure mountains follow the flow of the current.

Ascending the peak of Mount Bian, the summit stands firm with its crags unexposed. Clouds sleep and rocks roar, having done so for many years. Do not let your feet tread upon the moon at the tips of the pines;
lest you startle the flying rosy clouds across the ten-thousand-li sky.

Autumn Thoughts: A Single Laughter Resounds Through Heaven and Earth; Autumn pervades everywhere. White clouds and yellow leaves fill the vast marshlands. In the frosty sky, geese pass by, leaving their cries as shadows;
at dawn, the sun devours the mist, its light overflowing. A solitary peak conceals the rocks as it roars while swallowing the moon; ten thousand miles away, the clouds fly with great momentum.
The loach is contained within; who painted the emerald hue of the lotus? It remains for the world as a topic of discourse.

Regarding these matters, my two brows are already dyed with frost and snow; ten thousand autumns have passed, yet my constant mind has not been tamed. A single fragment of colored cloud is entirely internal.
The scene: when shall I reach the moon’s frosty orb?

Before the window, he joyfully wields his brush with flowing ink. That path, traversing vertically and horizontally, is a marvel of a thousand ages. His wind-bone spirit soars—whom else could attain it?
Against the void, dot by dot, he paints the brows of men.
The Thousand Pines Notes (Conclusion)
